hints: Look closely at the shape of each 18-carbon chain and count how many little kinks (bent double bonds) you can see in A, B, C and D.
Remember that each cis double bond puts a permanent kink in the tail that stops phospholipids packing tightly together, so think about which number of kinks pushes neighbours furthest apart.
walkthrough:
**Spot saturated versus unsaturated tails**

Look at the zig-zag lines. A is completely straight with no double bonds, so it is saturated. B, C and D have 1, 2 and 3 bent double bonds, so they are unsaturated.

Think: straight = can pack, kinked = cannot pack.

**Link kinks to membrane fluidity**

In a phospholipid bilayer, straight tails fit neatly together with strong hydrophobic interactions. This makes the membrane more rigid and less fluid.

Each cis double bond creates a kink that pushes neighbouring tails apart, weakens those interactions, and lets the phospholipids move more. More kinks means more fluidity.

**Pick the most kinked chain**

Count the double bonds: A has 0, B has 1, C has 2, D has 3. D has the most kinks, so its phospholipids pack the least well and move the most freely.

That is why D contributes most to fluidity.

options.A: This is a saturated fatty acid with a straight chain and no double bonds, so it packs very tightly and makes the membrane least fluid.
options.B: This has only one double bond and one kink, so it increases fluidity a little compared to A, but much less than C or D.
options.C: This has two double bonds and two kinks, so it increases fluidity more than B, but still less than D which has three.
options.D: This has three double bonds and three kinks, giving the most bent tail, the poorest packing, and therefore the greatest membrane fluidity.
